q1.question: What’s made you want to change things now?

options.label: Getting my work or my career unstuck
Being more present for my family
Changing the way I handle my relationships
Ending the feeling that money never lasts
Understanding why I keep ending up in the same place

q2.question: Have you tried to make a change, only to slip back into the same routine?

options.label: Yes, plenty of times
Yes, once
No, this is my first real shot

q3.question: Where has this been showing up in your life?

options.label: Feeling alone — like nobody gets it
How I see myself
Money or work
My health — body or mind
Relationships or my social life
None of these fits right now

q4.question: What feels like the biggest obstacle right now?

options.label: Old pain I still carry
Constant fear or worry
No money, or shaky work
I'm worn out — body and mind
Something I picked up as a kid
Boredom, or no real point to any of it

q5.question: Has any of this ever run through your head?

options.label: “I'm not enough. That's why it never works.”
“I'm scared to get it and lose it again.”
“No matter what I do, I end up back in the same place.”
“Even with people around, I'm alone in this.”
None of these — honestly, I don't know what it is

q6.question: Right now, do you feel like you've got real support for this?

options.label: Yes — family and close friends
Yes — groups or communities online
No — I'm doing this on my own

q7.question: How old are you?
q7.hint: Optional. Age does not affect your reflection. This preview is written for adults.

q8.question: If things started moving forward, what would matter most?

options.label: I'd finally move on the career I want
I'd be there, for real, with the people I love
I'd have relationships that work, without the same old loop
I'd feel calm and sure of myself again

q9.question: Have you heard of belief or subconscious reprogramming?

options.label: Yes, and I think it works
I've heard of it, but I have my doubts
No, this is new to me

q9.hint: Your answer only changes the optional activity that follows.

q10.question: Imagine making progress on this. How would you mark the moment?

options.label: A good dinner, just me
The trip I keep putting off
Something that marks the turn
I'd rather not say — but I know what it'd be

q10.hint: Picture something meaningful to you. This is a possibility to reflect on, not a promised outcome.

screen_0.title: What keeps getting between you and your next move?
body: You can want a change and still put it off. A money decision. A work conversation. Something you keep promising yourself you’ll do.
Answer 10 questions about what happens in those moments. You’ll get a reflection based on your answers and a written practice to help you choose where to begin.
screen_0.note: Free. No email needed. Go back and change any answer.

reinforcement_1.title: It’s hard to move forward when everything feels tangled.
body: The practical problem and what you tell yourself about it can become one big worry. “I need to look at the numbers” turns into “I’m terrible with money.” A work setback turns into “I’ll never be ready.”
Your answers give us a place to begin. Keep one recent moment in mind as you look at the thought that tends to follow it.

engine_reveal_q5.title: A theme is showing up again.
engine_reveal_q5.body: The thought you selected echoes a theme in your earlier answers. That connection can be useful to explore; it does not establish what caused it.

reinforcement_2.title: What would make this change worth it to you?
body: You’ve described what gets in the way and who you can turn to. Now bring it back to your own life.
It might be a work decision you finally make, a conversation you stop avoiding, or some time that feels like yours again. The next questions help shape an example you can work with.

engine_reveal_q8.title: That connects with where you started.
engine_reveal_q8.body: Your first answer and the change you want both point to the same part of your life. We’ll use that context in your reflection.

priming_2.title: Try one small observation.
priming_2.intro: This optional activity illustrates attention and imagination. It does not test for a hidden block or prove that reprogramming works.

believer.body: If you like, picture lighting an incense stick. Imagine the smoke rising and a scent you associate with it. You can keep your eyes open. It is fine if no image or scent comes to mind.
believer.question: Did anything come to mind?

doubter.body: Pause for a moment and notice how you are sitting. Is there an area that feels tense, relaxed, or simply neutral? You do not need to change anything or find a particular sensation.
doubter.question: Did you notice a sensation?

skeptic.body: When you read “stuck”, which word comes to mind? Take as much time as you want. Your choice is an association, not a test of your personality.
skeptic.question: Did a word feel relevant to your situation?

options.label: Yes
Somewhat
No

result_lines.believer: In the optional activity, you noticed an image or association. You can use that same pause to notice the thought that comes with a real situation.
result_lines.doubter: In the optional activity, you noticed a sensation. You can choose whether noticing how you feel is useful before preparing a response.
result_lines.skeptic: In the optional activity, a word felt relevant to you. If it helps, use it as a starting point for describing one real situation.

reinforcement_3.title: A clearer picture needs a practical next step.
body: We call the interruption between an intention and a response {{MECHANISM}}. Think of it as a way to describe the moment you want to understand.
Protocol 44 works with situations you can put into words. The first practice takes you through these three parts.

cards.title: A situation you can describe
cards.body: Start with an actual request, decision or interrupted plan.

cards.title: A response you can prepare
cards.body: Give yourself words or a next step that fits your circumstances.

cards.title: A way to return
cards.body: Keep a smaller option available when the first plan no longer fits.

citations.name: Dweck & Leggett · 1988

citations.body: A theoretical account of how goals and beliefs relate to patterns of motivation and behaviour. It does not establish an invisible signal or validate this reflection.

citations.name: Hiroto & Seligman · 1975
citations.title: Responses after uncontrollable events
citations.body: Laboratory experiments examined transfer of helplessness across tasks. The paper does not demonstrate that this program can remove a personal block.

concrete_lack.name: Money and stability
concrete_lack.title: Turn the money worry into a decision you can work on.
concrete_lack.intro: Money, work or stability came up in your answers. Start with the decision that keeps returning to your mind, then separate what you know from what you still need to find out.
concrete_lack.recognition: A bill you have not opened. A conversation about pay. An opportunity that feels too uncertain to explore. When the whole situation becomes one big worry, even the first step can be difficult to see.
concrete_lack.mechanism: Here, {{MECHANISM}} is a metaphor for what interrupts a practical decision. Separate the circumstances you face from the conclusion you draw about yourself. Then identify what you can find out or do next.
concrete_lack.before: The money task stays open. A general worry replaces the next decision.
concrete_lack.after: Name one question. Find a reliable record or person who can help answer it.
concrete_lack.prompt: What is one fact you need before making the money or work decision you have been postponing?
concrete_lack.next: For this practice, choose one information task you can manage. It gives you something to work with; it does not guarantee a financial outcome.

scenes.professional: A work decision has been circling for days. Write the question you need answered, the information already available, and the next person or record to consult.
scenes.family: A shared expense keeps coming back into conversation. Put the known amounts and unanswered questions in one place before choosing what to discuss.
scenes.relational: Money is making a conversation harder. Prepare one practical question and distinguish it from assumptions about what the other person thinks.

concrete_lack.metaphor: Think of trying to hear one voice in a noisy room. In the practice, you set one situation apart from everything around it: the facts, the thought that followed, and the response you want to prepare.

health_burnout.name: Energy and capacity
health_burnout.title: Make room for the next move you can actually manage.
health_burnout.intro: Tiredness, health or limited capacity featured in your answers. Start with one demand you could clarify, reduce or ask for help with.
health_burnout.recognition: You agree to one more thing. By the time you return to your own plan, there is very little left to give it. Put that demand into words and look at what it will take before deciding what you can offer.
health_burnout.mechanism: Here, {{MECHANISM}} is a metaphor for the gap between a demand and the capacity you have. Look at the request, the assumptions around it and what you could reasonably offer.
health_burnout.before: A request arrives. You agree before checking what it will displace.
health_burnout.after: Check your capacity. Prepare a limit, a question or a request for support.
health_burnout.prompt: What is one demand you could clarify, reduce or ask for help with?
health_burnout.next: A clearer response is one practical step. Persistent or concerning symptoms deserve appropriate professional attention; this reflection cannot assess their cause.

scenes.family: A family responsibility leaves little room in the day. Identify the part you can do and one specific form of help you could request.
scenes.relational: You keep being available for a conversation when you need a pause. Prepare a time you can offer and say clearly when you need to stop.

internal_block.name: Recurring thoughts and expectations
internal_block.title: Catch the thought that keeps putting your next move on hold.
internal_block.intro: Familiar thoughts and expectations came up in your answers. Look at one moment when a thought changed what you did next.
internal_block.recognition: “I’m not ready.” “I should be able to handle this.” “I never follow through.” Put the actual sentence on paper, beside the situation that brought it up. You can examine it without having to explain your whole history.
internal_block.mechanism: Here, {{MECHANISM}} is a metaphor for an interpretation that cuts into a choice. Put the event and the interpretation in separate sentences. That gives you something specific to question and a response to prepare.
internal_block.before: A plan is interrupted. “I never follow through” becomes the reason to stop.
internal_block.after: Name the interruption. Keep one useful step and choose a way back.
internal_block.prompt: What did you tell yourself after the last setback, and what else was happening at the time?
internal_block.next: You can examine a familiar rule without knowing its entire history. Your next response can take account of what matters to you and what is possible now.

scenes.relational: You want to say what you need, then predict the other person’s response. Separate what you know from what you expect and prepare a sentence you could adapt.

mixed.title: You can begin before you have it all figured out.
mixed.intro: Your answers do not point clearly to one theme. Money, capacity and familiar thoughts can overlap. This reflection will keep the starting point open.

home.title: Stop putting your next move on hold | {{BRAND}}
home.description: Make a clearer decision about money or work. Explore Protocol 44, take the free quiz and try the first written practice.
headline: Stop putting your
next move
on hold.
home.intro: The money decision. The career move. The conversation you keep rehearsing. Give one of them a next step you can actually take.
home.body: Protocol 44 is a guided personal development program for understanding what interrupts your decisions, preparing a different response, and following through when life gets in the way.
home.note: 10 questions. A personal reflection. A free first practice. No email needed.
home.status: The full program is in preparation. The written preview is free to try now.
home.photoAlt: A woman writing in a notebook at a kitchen table in afternoon light
recognitionBody: You open the job listing, then close it. Put the bill aside until you feel ready. Say yes to another request while your own plan waits. The decision stays with you long after the moment has passed.

Start there. What happened just before you put it off? What did you tell yourself? What information, support or response would help you move forward? Protocol 44 gives you a way to work through those questions.
insideTitle: A way to work through it.
insideBody: The planned program brings together 22 video sessions and 22 guided audio practices in three phases. Keep a real situation in view as you learn, rehearse and review.

Bring the job conversation, the money task or the boundary you keep postponing. Build a written picture of what gets in the way, words for your next response, and a plan for returning when a week goes sideways.

phases.name: The Reading
phases.title: See what interrupts the decision.
phases.body: Describe a recent moment. Separate what happened from what you assumed, and examine familiar rules about money, responsibility and approval.
phases.output: Your situation, clearly on the page.

phases.name: The Move
phases.title: Choose words. Prepare an action.
phases.body: Rehearse the question, boundary or next step you have been postponing. Include the time, information and support it will require.
phases.output: A response you can use in real life.

phases.name: The Hold
phases.title: Keep one setback from ending the plan.
phases.body: Review what happened when you tried. Adjust what did not fit and choose a smaller way back after an interruption.
phases.output: A next attempt you can return to.

home.exampleBody: Maya missed one spending review, then avoided her notebook for a week. The practice looks at the thought and decision that followed the missed session.
home.exampleDisclosure: Maya is a fictional example from the first written sample.

exampleSteps.label: What happened
exampleSteps.title: She missed her Sunday review.
exampleSteps.body: Maya planned ten minutes to review the week’s expenses. A family visit ran late, and she missed her usual time.

exampleSteps.label: What she thought
exampleSteps.title: “I never stick with this.”
exampleSteps.body: That is what Maya told herself the next morning. She avoided the notebook for the rest of the week.

exampleSteps.label: What she could try
exampleSteps.title: Open the notebook. Check one bill.
exampleSteps.body: On Monday, Maya can take one small step and schedule the rest of the review separately.
exampleSteps.prompt: Choose something she could do now.

faqs.q: What will I get from the quiz?
faqs.a: A reflection calculated from the themes in your answers, a practical question and a written activity to begin with. It is free and appears here. No email is required.

faqs.q: What if I’ve tried something like this before?
faqs.a: See what you’ll actually do. The sample asks you to describe a setback, notice the thought that followed, and choose a specific response. Try it before deciding whether the approach fits you.

faqs.q: What if the reflection doesn’t feel right?
faqs.a: Review your answers or start with a situation that feels more useful. The quiz groups selected themes; it does not establish a hidden cause or tell you who you are.

faqs.q: How will the audio practices work?
faqs.a: Each planned audio is paired with a video session. It guides reflection and rehearsal, with pauses to consider your situation. You then choose an action and review it in your notes. Recordings are in preparation.
It is still in preparation. The first written sample is available now. The final schedule, access terms and support details will be shared before enrollment opens.

practice.title: Leave with a next step.
practice.intro: Write about one moment you want to handle differently. A sentence or two per question is enough. You can leave a question open and come back to it.
example: In this fictional example, Maya planned to review her spending on Sunday. A family visit ran late. She thought, “I never stick with this,” and put her notebook away.
Her next step: open the notebook on Monday and check one upcoming bill. She can schedule the rest separately.

sectionBody: You planned to do something for yourself. The day changed, and the plan slipped. Then came the thought: “I never follow through.”
The practice puts those pieces on paper: the event, your interpretation, and your next move. Include practical constraints such as time, money or responsibilities. They matter.
You might ask for time before saying yes, open one bill, or choose when to return to a plan. Pick a step small enough to try, and decide when you’ll review it.

faqs.q: What if I don’t know why I do this?
faqs.a: You can leave that question open. Write about something you remember and what you noticed at the time. You don’t need an explanation for everything.

faqs.q: What if I can’t do what I planned?
faqs.a: Choose a smaller step or a different time. If you planned to review your spending, opening a bill might be enough to get started. Adjust the plan to what’s possible.

faqs.q: How do I know when I’m done?
faqs.a: You’re done when you’ve described the situation and chosen something to try next. Come back to your notes afterward and see what you would change.
The form does not send your writing anywhere or keep it after the page is reloaded. Use “Download my reflection” to save a text file on your device.
